KSP2.title: 13-year-old Carlsen vs Kasparov #shorts
KSP2.desc:
In March 2004 at a rapid tournament in Reykjavik, 13-year-old Magnus Carlsen (rated 2484) played Garry Kasparov, the world number one (2831). The day before, he had beaten former world champion Anatoly Karpov in a blitz game. Against Kasparov the boy had White and pressed him for most of the game; Kasparov only just escaped with a draw, and then he won the second game. Nine years later, Carlsen became world champion himself.

In 2022 he said he wasn't motivated to play another title match, and he gave up the title. These days he plays a lot of blitz online, and thousands of fans watch him live on stream. In 2025 he won Titled Tuesday, the weekly online blitz event, with eleven wins out of eleven (in April, and again on 11 November, the night of the stream in this video). He also helped start Freestyle Chess, where the back row is shuffled before each game. Another new version keeps the usual start: Joker Chess. Once per game, each player can jump a queen, rook, bishop or knight to any empty square. Maybe one day he'll try it on stream.
Free on iPhone and Android: joker-chess.com

Who would you rather play at 13, Karpov or Kasparov?

NKM2.title: He threw the world champion's king into the crowd #shorts
NKM2.desc:
On 4 October 2025, at the Checkmate: USA vs India show match in an esports stadium in Arlington, Texas, Hikaru Nakamura checkmated world champion Gukesh and threw his king into the crowd. About a thousand fans watched it. The organizers had planned the throw, but many players called it disrespectful. Earlier that year, at Norway Chess, Magnus Carlsen slammed the table after losing to Gukesh. A few weeks after the throw, Gukesh beat Nakamura in St. Louis.

The game in the first seconds is the real one: Nakamura–Gukesh, 1.b4 … 56.Qd8#. Their first two games that night were draws, so they played a third, even faster one, and Gukesh allowed a mate in one just when he could have repeated moves for another draw. Some called that night a peek at the future of chess. Others think the future is a small change to the rules: in Joker Chess, each player gets one jump per game, to any empty square. One jump like that might even have saved Gukesh from that mate.
Free on iPhone and Android: joker-chess.com

Funny or disrespectful?

RAU2.title: Caught with a phone in the tournament toilet #shorts
RAU2.desc:
In July 2019, at a tournament in Strasbourg, 58-year-old grandmaster Igors Rausis was caught with his phone in the toilet; someone took a photo of him on the toilet with the phone. He had climbed almost 200 rating points in six years, which made him the oldest player in the world's top 100. He signed that the phone was his and admitted to cheating. He lost his grandmaster title and got a six-year ban.

A phone app now plays better than any human, so one look at a screen can decide a game. One idea is faster chess, because in blitz there's no time to leave the board. Top events also scan the players for devices and show the moves with a 15-minute delay (the Sinquefield Cup added both in 2022). Another idea is a version of chess that the big engines don't know yet: in Joker Chess, each player gets one jump per game, to any empty square. Stockfish wasn't built for that, so a phone in the toilet won't help much.
Free on iPhone and Android: joker-chess.com

How should chess stop cheaters?

JNS2.title: Carlsen was fined for wearing jeans #shorts
JNS2.desc:
In December 2024, at the World Rapid Championship in New York, Magnus Carlsen was fined 200 dollars for wearing jeans. He refused to change, so he was left out of the next round, and he quit the event. Days later the dress code was relaxed, and he came back for the World Blitz in jeans. In the final he played Ian Nepomniachtchi, and they drew three games in a row, so Carlsen suggested they share the title, and for the first time ever, they did. Later he sold the jeans on eBay for 36,100 dollars, and the money went to charity.

The rules on the board change much more slowly: the pieces have moved the same way for about 500 years. Carlsen wants to shake that up too, and he co-founded Freestyle Chess, where the back row is shuffled. Joker Chess changes even less and keeps the usual start: once per game, each player can jump a queen, rook, bishop or knight to any empty square. And you can play it in jeans.
Free on iPhone and Android: joker-chess.com

Should chess have a dress code?

HOU2.title: The women's world champion lost in five moves, on purpose #shorts
HOU2.desc:
On 2 February 2017, in the last round of the Gibraltar Masters, women's world champion Hou Yifan came 25 minutes late to her game against Lalith Babu, opened with 1.g4, followed with more bad moves and resigned after five moves. It was a protest: she had been paired with seven women in her first nine games. The organizers said a computer made the pairings, and she later apologized to the fans. It's still the fastest loss by a grandmaster on record.

A year later she stepped back from top chess to study at Oxford, and in July 2020, at 26, she became the youngest full professor at Shenzhen University. That protest game broke every rule of a good opening. Joker Chess breaks only one rule, and only once per game: a queen, rook, bishop or knight can jump to any empty square, without capturing or giving check. Two friends came up with it at a wooden board, and now it's a free app.
Free on iPhone and Android: joker-chess.com

Was her protest fair?

NMN2.title: Carlsen vs Niemann: the game that started it all #shorts
NMN2.desc:
On 4 September 2022 at the Sinquefield Cup in St. Louis, 19-year-old Hans Niemann beat world champion Magnus Carlsen with Black. The next day Carlsen quit the tournament and hinted that Niemann had cheated. Two weeks later they met again online, and Carlsen resigned after one move. Niemann admitted cheating online as a kid, but he denied ever cheating over the board. He sued for 100 million dollars; the case was dismissed, and in 2023 both sides settled. Carlsen said there was no clear proof that Niemann cheated in their game.

In January 2024 they met online again, in Titled Tuesday: after 28 moves only kings and pawns were left, they kept going for 59 more moves, and it still ended in a draw. Later that year in Paris they finally played in the same room again, for the first time since St. Louis 2022, in the Speed Chess Championship semifinal, and Carlsen won 17½–12½. If they ever meet again, they could try a version that nobody can prepare at home: Joker Chess, where once per game a piece can jump to any empty square. Two friends came up with it at a wooden board, and now it's a free app.
Free on iPhone and Android: joker-chess.com

What do you think happened?

BNG2.title: Carlsen played the worst move in chess #shorts
BNG2.desc:
On 15 March 2021, in the last preliminary round of the online Magnus Carlsen Invitational, world champion Magnus Carlsen pushed his king's pawn and then walked his king forward with 2.Ke2, the Bongcloud, an opening that started as an internet joke. Hikaru Nakamura answered by walking his king out too. Both of them had already qualified for the next stage, so the game didn't matter. They moved their kings back and forth, and after six moves it was a draw by repetition.

Months earlier, in the final of the chess24 Banter Series (29 September 2020), Carlsen opened against Wesley So with 1.f3 and 2.Kf2, and still won the game; So said losing to it was humiliating. Hikaru Nakamura has even won with the Bongcloud itself, against Jeffery Xiong at the 2020 St. Louis Rapid & Blitz. At the top, a silly opening is one of the few surprises left. Joker Chess gives every player one surprise like that per game: a queen, rook, bishop or knight can jump to any empty square, without capturing or giving check. And the king can stay at home.
Free on iPhone and Android: joker-chess.com

Have you ever played the Bongcloud?

DBL2.title: The day a computer beat the world chess champion #shorts
DBL2.desc:
In May 1997 in New York, IBM's Deep Blue beat world champion Garry Kasparov 3.5-2.5, the first time a computer won a match against a reigning world champion. A year earlier in Philadelphia, Kasparov had beaten Deep Blue four games to two. For the rematch the machine was made much stronger: it could look at about 200 million positions every second. In the deciding sixth game Kasparov resigned after just 19 moves. He hinted that humans had helped the machine and asked for another match, but IBM said no, and Deep Blue never played again.

Deep Blue also had an opening book, prepared for it by grandmasters. With the pieces shuffled, like in Fischer's chess, that book would have been useless from move one. Joker Chess breaks the script in a different way, with one jump per player: a queen, rook, bishop or knight can jump to any empty square, without capturing or giving check. Would Kasparov have had a better chance? Nobody will ever know.
Free on iPhone and Android: joker-chess.com

Could a human still beat a computer today?

KVW3.title: One man vs the whole world #shorts
KVW3.desc:
In 1999, Garry Kasparov played one game of chess against the whole world. He had White, and more than 50,000 people from 75 countries voted on every Black move. The game was played online and took four months. A 15-year-old American champion, Irina Krush, led the analysis for the world team, and on move ten the world played a brand new move that she had suggested.
